timid

/TIM-id/ — rhymes with vim · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Timid describes someone who is shy and lacks confidence, especially in new or uncertain situations.

The timid new student ate lunch alone rather than ask to join a table.

Example

The timid intern barely spoke during the team meeting, despite having prepared thoughtful comments, because she feared being judged or saying something wrong.

Timid captures the combination of shyness and lack of confidence, which is more precise than just calling someone 'quiet' or 'anxious.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

meek: Meek means quietly gentle and mild — a meek person accepts what others decide and will not argue or push back. Timid is about fear rather than gentleness: a timid person may badly want to act or speak, but nervous lack of confidence holds them back.

bashful: Bashful means easily embarrassed in front of people — blushing, ducking your head, hating to be noticed. It is about self-consciousness, not fear. Timid runs deeper: a timid person is held back by real nervousness and lack of confidence, even when nobody is watching them.

fainthearted: Fainthearted means lacking the courage to face something risky or frightening — the nerve fails exactly when boldness is required. Timid is broader and quieter: shyness and low confidence that hold a person back even in everyday situations where no real danger is involved.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

bold: confident and eager to take risks

assertive: confidently stating what you want or think

Where it sits · how much fear holds someone back — quiet → shy → diffident → timid

quiet vs. timid: Quiet is far weaker than timid: a quiet person may simply prefer silence, while a timid person stays silent because confidence fails them.

shy vs. timid: Shy is weaker than timid; a shy student hesitates around new people, but a timid one is held back by nervous fear in almost any uncertain situation.

diffident vs. timid: Diffident comes close to timid, but timid is stronger — diffidence is quietly doubting your own abilities, while timidity adds real fearfulness that keeps you from acting at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — tim

Root — tim: to fear (Latin)

Suffix — -id

Suffix — -id: having the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Timid combines the Latin root tim-, from timere, 'to fear,' with the adjective suffix -id, 'having the quality of' — literally 'full of fear,' describing someone whose shyness and hesitation come from a lack of confidence.

Use the root in a new word: intimidate
